story_text.value:
Hi HN, we're the co-founders of Acyclic (YC F26).

Acyclic runs any agentic workflow as a swarm. You give it a task and your project; it splits the work across many coding agents, each in its own sandbox, runs them in parallel, and merges what they produce into one patch or pull request.

Our thesis: agentic workflows should be realtime, no matter how complex the task. The bottleneck should be human ideation and design, whilst building happens at the speed of thought.

To bring this to you we make our agents recursively fork and speculative execute. This means that if an agent has 2 independent tasks to do, it will just split into 2 agents to solve both tasks quickly and merge back up the tree. Additionally, for sequential operations we have “speculative” agents which guess the next steps of the workflow as a pre-fetch step.

To make this efficient we are solving the infrastructure bottlenecks. We are solving the memory, communication, routing and durable execution issues. This infra is open source at acyclic.dev/github, so check it out!

To run your own swarm (check out acyclic.dev for a full guide)

``` npm install -g @acyclic-labs/cli acyclic swarm run --task <prompt> --dir <files_to_upload> ```

A good (non-coding) first task to try out: Do deep research into a person. “Do deep research into Jeff Goldblum“ You can view the results at acyclic.dev/dashboard or stream the results back to the cli using:

``` acyclic swarm pull <swarm-id> --apply ```

Check out some more research examples at acyclic.dev/evals, right now our biggest useful swarm is 236 agents for a code migration.

title.value: Show HN: Acyclic; Rapid agent swarms

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I partnered with Simon Kley to build this project at innovation intelligence hackathon (Berkeley).

Simply, we’re building a usefulness score on top of search for ai-agents.

Instead of agents reading 10 ranked relevant pages, we run a usefulness score first and give it only those that pass. We’re able to save token and cost with this and slightly better answers.

During our research, we found out that the current search results already do justice when it comes to simple queries. The rankings work well. They struggle when the task requires deep research or recency matters. So, we decided to talk to devs building ai-agents that research companies for sales outreach. Deep research and recency matters a lot to them. And in their words “every so often, stale facts reach emails.” They catch them by someone responding to the email or human review.

From our tests, When an agent got outdated alert for 7 companies, it pitched outdated news for 4 out of them.

Talking to the engineers already building this agents, we learned that cost saving is not the real goal. They’re ready to pay premium for confident results. So we added another check to our score. We call it superseding score, it check for pages replaced by newer news. For example, if two recent pages were fetched for news on Humane ai pin. If the first talks about how groundbreaking the product is and the second did that + talked about the HP acquisition, then the second page supersedes the first. The first page gets a lower score.

We’re looking for feedbacks here and also teams that are building agents that research companies for outreach. Thanks.

Plus, we rank a page once and every agent reuses it, so the more the agents use us, the cheaper the search gets.

title.value: Show HN: Search for AI agents with usefulness score built in

story_text.value:
I was under the impression that for doing any research we humans require emotions which AI truly lacks. But with how AI going autonomously I fail to understand how that could be even possible without emotions.

Are AI really curious to do something on its own? I am not an AI critic but fail to understand this nuance of not being emotional and doing deep research beating highly emotional human researchers on their field. How is this even possible by an advanced pattern matcher with reinforcement learning? From where it gets its curiosity to go autonomous?

Also can we say AI as trained professionals especially given its non deterministic stochastic nature? Despite that randomness how do they beat human professionals on their field? Does math have solution to all our questions? I understand that this AI is an illusion but how it alters our brain waves when we interact with it.

Please help me to enlighten others and make us understand the "AI Behavior".

title.value: Don't we require emotions for doing research?

story_text.value:
My kid just started high school. The way they communicate information is absolutely insane. So I built a web scraper + MCP to aggregate it all, then layered on a snarky chatbot with a PG-13 Dave Chappelle personality.

The number of communication channels are just insane: - email - Google Docs - Canvas - PDFs - School Messenger - the official school website - 5 different other websites that they don't tell you about (eg athletics website) - 22 (!) Instagram accounts for various school clubs & sports - district website & calendar

Oh, and if you call the school office, they say "look at the website" or "that's handled by a different department." The whole system is just insane.

So I did something about it. With AI. Last weekend.

- Scraper: indexes all the public PDFs, GDocs, websites and Instagram accounts they have 4x per school day. It even transcribes images, because yes, they announce important deadlines over Instagram... as images!!! <dies inside> - MCP server: makes all of the above available to any AI. - Chatbot: Gemini 3.7 Flash with a "PG-13 Dave Chappelle" persona that answers legit questions helpfully and cracks jokes. All answers are grounded in the MCP and web search as a fallback. Trolls you if you go off-topic. Threatens to lookup your IP and report you to the principal if you ask for homework help. Prompt is loaded with deep research on the school and surrounding area as a fodder for jokes.

It's awesome. I'm proud. And finally I know what the hell is going on with my kid's school!

title.value: Show HN: Tesoro.help – rogue AI helpdesk for my kid's high school

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

We're finally launching Votito, after about a year of development, as it's now (almost) polished enough for other people to use. I'd love your feedback!

AI tools make software faster to write, so the constraint is no longer building things. It is knowing which things deserve to be built. Votito aims to be a "product decision platform" to help figure that out.

Having previously built two relatively successful SaaS products, we've spent a ton of time figuring out what users need, collecting feedback and trying to turn signals from the user community into actionable ideas, using a bunch of disconnected tools and half-baked scripts. We've consolidated those internal tools and processes into an online idea management system, combining user feedback with product research, so product teams can engage their users easily.

Votito is not trying to compete with task management tools like Jira and Linear, but to work in the area before the backlog, in the "weak commitment" zone where unstructured proposals need to mature to become implementable ideas. Throw random stakeholder demands, user suggestions and feature requests into Votito and let them marinate until they become something useful, if they ever do. Votito will help you spot the gems that deserve your attention. It will also stop garbage from going into your actual task tracking tools, and prevent people from being overwhelmed with managing bad ideas.

While the product is naturally oriented towards PMs, we're betting on the trend that teams are becoming smaller with AI support, and that people inside delivery teams will need to take on most traditional product responsibilities in the future. The Wall Street Journal recently reported on the trend of "pods" of 3-4 people augmented with AI agents taking on the tasks that previously needed much larger groups. When teams have 10-15 people, companies can justify assigning a dedicated product person. But with 3-4 people per pod, this is just not feasible. GitHub's research from December 2025 found that developers will increasingly need to think at the level of "understanding user needs".

One of our goals is to put proven product methods and tools into the hands of people who are not traditional product managers, making it easy to discover and apply the right tools and, crucially, to understand the results.

Here are 5 ways Votito can help you decide what to build next:

- Collect evidence with ideas to help you prove that things are worth building. Evidence can be as simple as a list of interested customers, external documents such as market research, or something as complex as the result of an A/B test.

- Score ideas automatically based on impact, effort and evidence. We provide two popular confidence models out of the box to help you get started.

- Engage users or stakeholders to vote on ideas for additional confidence signals.

- Keep the community engaged. Let people propose new ideas directly in Votito, comment and vote on other people's proposals. Publishing a roadmap of ideas you've accepted into development, and a changelog of features you delivered recently.

- Conduct deep research with proven product management surveys. Feature requests are pointers that something is interesting, but they are rarely complete information, or even the best solutions for the problem. Votito allows you to easily run online surveys with people who voted on a proposal. We provide a collection of ready-made templates for major product management research tasks. You could, of course, set up a similar survey on another platform, but the difference is that we'll help you interpret the data, showing the best ways to score domain-specific surveys and evaluate statistical significance.

The free version includes pretty much everything you need to run all the things mentioned above, with data retention of up to six months.

title.value: Show HN: Votito helps you decide what to build next with confidence

story_text.value:
Doing research with agents is fun until they blow way past budget, jumble the sources, and don't even give you the best possible answer, just sound confident.

And if you want to run some research task on local data - you have no idea where your data ends up after the prompt consumes it.

So I built this tool: a deep-research agent with an enforced budget, verified quotes, and a privacy boundary for local data.

1. Never spend more than you budgeted (measured overshoot is 0%). 2. Every claim carries a source 3. Data stays local (give a CSV, it'll analyze it without the data ever leaving your machine)

Works with most LLMs, including coding agents, subscriptions, local models, etc.

It's free and open source, would appreciate all feedback!

title.value: Show HN: Mole – Deep research agent for your terminal

story_text.value:
*Title:* Show HN: FutureSearch, AI forecasting you can verify

AI forecasting is now approximately superhuman. Today, FutureSearch is exiting our long public beta and launching.

We started FutureSearch in August 2023. (We’re the original AI forecasting company, at least in a Tetlock-ian, “forecast anything” sense.) We’re currently #1 of 194 in the most competitive AI forecasting tournament [1], and we score above the #3 and #2 human forecasters in the premier mixed human-bot tournaments [2].

Many people on HN seem to equate forecasting with prediction markets and finance. FutureSearch is not a financial tool, in the same way that “deep research” is not a financial tool. Yes, we do evaluate our forecaster on prediction markets [3]. But forecasting is about being as accurate about the future as possible, and the real game is in forecasting scientific progress, geopolitics, and the future of humanity. Our founding team came from Metaculus, where we pushed human forecasting to the limit on questions like when AGI would arrive. At. FutureSearch, we co-authored the AI 2027 timeline forecast, where we predicted superhuman coding and research would come around 2032, longer than the other authors, but still shorter than skeptics [4].

Thousands of people used the FutureSearch beta and ran >10k high-effort forecasts, on all sorts of diverse topics. Ask it anything about the future. We now support decision forecasts too: “If I do X, will I achieve this outcome?”

Forecasting, as a capability, is useful even at the level of expert human crowds. But we predict that we will soon have strongly superhuman forecasting. People who bet against AI capability trend lines tend to lose, and the trend line in AI forecast accuracy tells a pretty clear story [5]. There’s no reason to think the best human forecasters have figured out everything predictable about the world. There’s a lot more signal to be found.

And if you’re skeptical, try it. We’ve seen our fair share of exaggerated claims about AI forecasting accuracy [6]. So part of the reason we made the free tier give a few of our highest effort forecasters free is to let anyone verify the quality.

[1] https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/summer-futureeval-2026/ [2] evals.futuresearch.ai [3] markets.futuresearch.ai [4] https://ai-2027.com/research/timelines-forecast [5] https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-superforecasters-are... [6] https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/uGkRcHqatmPkvpGLq/contra-pap...

title.value: Show HN: FutureSearch, AI forecasting you can verify

story_text.value: Abendrot is a handcrafted application designed for the burners of the midnight oil. I got tired of spending night after night staring into a luminous computer screen blasting blue-rich light at my eyes long after sunset. After a long deep research session with frontier models, the need for Abendrot became apparent. macOS can warm displays natively with Night Shift but it is nowhere near where it needs to be for optimal blue light reduction.
